fields.h1: Build a Maintenance Request Form Your Team Acts On
fields.hero_description: Describe the buildings you look after and who fixes what. Emergent builds the maintenance request form, ranks each report by urgency and tracks it until the repair is closed.
fields.features_heading: What a Request Form Settles First
fields.features_subheading: Most request forms collect a name and a complaint. These six pieces decide what happens in the hour after someone presses submit.
fields.feature_1:
Locations picked from your own list

Let people choose the building, floor and room from a list you control instead of typing an address. Reports arrive with clean locations you can sort and filter by site.
fields.feature_2:
Urgency set by what the problem stops

Rank each issue type by what it takes out of use, such as a guest room or a kitchen line. A report that stops work or a sale is flagged urgent before anyone reads it.
fields.feature_3:
Photos taken with the phone camera

Add a required photo field that opens the camera on a phone. A picture of the leak or the error code tells the technician which part to carry before the first visit.
fields.feature_4:
Duplicate reports folded together

Match new reports against open ones by location and category. A second report of the same broken latch joins the first request, and both people get the same updates.
fields.feature_5:
Escalation when nobody responds

Set how long a request may sit unacknowledged. Once that window passes, the app sends it to a named person in Slack or by email, with how long it waited and who filed it.
fields.feature_6:
Source code you can take with you

Export the full codebase to your GitHub repository when you want to tie requests to an asset register, or run the app on servers that your own team manages and patches.
fields.why_title: Why Build Maintenance Forms With Emergent?
fields.why_description: A printed form records the problem and stops. Someone still judges the urgency, finds who should fix it and chases the reply.

fields.usecase_heading: Requests in Four Kinds of Buildings
fields.tab_content_1:
A dead AC pulls room 418 from sale

At Halden House Hotel, a housekeeper reports a dead air conditioner in room 418 from her phone, with a photo of the thermostat. Anything that makes a room unusable marks it Out of order until engineering closes the request, and the front desk cannot assign it. A loose towel bar only marks a room Out of service.
fields.tab_content_2:
Three reports of one broken gate become one job

On a hot afternoon at Briar Glen, three residents report that the pool gate latch is broken. The form matches each report on location and category, then attaches the later ones to the first request. The pool vendor gets one job. Every reporter is emailed when the visit is booked and again when the latch is fixed.
fields.tab_content_3:
Cooler WC-02 hits three repairs and goes to review

Copperleaf Kitchen puts an asset tag on every piece of equipment, and the request form asks for it. When the Midtown kitchen manager logs a third repair on walk-in cooler WC-02 within 30 days, the unit is flagged for a replacement review. The operations director sees the $1,240 already spent on it.
fields.tab_content_4:
Four quiet hours send a request to the chief engineer

Fenwick Tower gives each tenant's office manager one link for requests. A jammed badge door on floor 9 sits for 4 business hours without anyone acknowledging it. The app then sends Dana Ortiz, the chief engineer, a direct message with the request and how long it has waited.

fields.howto_title: How to Create a Maintenance Request Form
fields.howto_description: Decide where requests come from and who answers them before you write a prompt.
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 Sort problems by what they stop
fields.howto_step_1_des: Write down every building, floor and room people will report from, or every asset if you track equipment. A pick list built from that inventory gives you clean locations. Duplicate matching and per-building reports both depend on it later.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Group issue types by impact instead of by trade. A leak over a bed or a dead walk-in cooler is urgent. A scuffed wall can wait for the next scheduled visit. Write that list down in plain words, one line per issue type.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Pick what a technician needs before leaving the shop: the exact spot and a photo. Make the rest optional. Each extra required field is one more reason for someone to skip the form and phone the front desk instead.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Choose how many hours can pass before someone acknowledges a request, then name the one person who hears about it after that. Four business hours suits most offices. A hotel with rooms off sale may want one hour.
fields.howto_step_5_des: Put your locations, issue types and rules into one prompt in plain English. Emergent builds the request form and a requests table behind it, along with the alerts. Change a rule later by asking for the change in the same chat.
fields.howto_step_6_title: 06 Connect the tools your team uses
fields.howto_step_6_des: Connect Slack or email for alerts. If requests should update an asset register or an accounting tool you already keep, connect that too. Any tool with an API can receive a new request or a closed one.
fields.howto_step_7_des: Open the form on a phone and report one urgent problem twice. Check that the first report alerts the right person and the second joins it instead of opening a new request. Then file a routine one and confirm it waits in the queue.
